lesson.text: Quick memory: what is an opportunity cost? (What you give up when you choose.) This year, prices can have parts of a gold coin, like 2.50 gold. Today: how to spend wisely.
The same thing can cost different amounts in different places. Tilly sells a kite for 6.50 gold, and Bram's stall has the same kite for 5.75 gold. 6.50 − 5.75 = 0.75, so Bram's is 0.75 gold cheaper.
Bigger packs are not always cheaper. Find the price for one: 4 apples for 2 gold is 0.50 gold each; 6 apples for 2.40 gold is 0.40 gold each. The bag of 6 is better value, if you will eat them all.
Cheapest is not always best. A 3-gold rope that breaks in a day is worse value than an 8-gold rope that lasts all year. Think about how long it lasts and how often you will use it.
Before buying, weigh the costs and the benefits. Costs: the price, and what else the gold could buy. Benefits: what it does for you. Buy when the benefits are worth more to you than the costs.
Every gold coin can only be spent once. If Mimi spends 10 gold on a hat, she can't spend it on the 10-gold book she also wanted. The book is her opportunity cost.
Adverts and shiny things make us want to buy right now. A smart trick: wait a day. If you still want it tomorrow, and it fits your plan, it may be a good buy.
Try it in the world: at the shop, compare two stalls before you buy, and work out the price for one in any pack. Next: adverts and you.

exercises.prompt: The same kite costs 6 gold at one stall and 4 gold at another. Which is cheaper?
choices: the stall selling it for 4 gold
the stall selling it for 6 gold
exercises.explain: 4 gold is less than 6 gold, so that stall is cheaper, by 2 gold.

exercises.prompt: The cheapest thing is always the best buy.
exercises.hint: Remember the rope that breaks in a day.
exercises.explain: False: a cheap thing that breaks fast can be worse value than a dearer thing that lasts.

choices: what you give up when you choose
exercises.explain: It is the next-best thing you give up when you choose.

exercises.prompt: What is a smart trick before buying something you suddenly want?
choices: wait a day, and see if you still want it
exercises.explain: Wait a day: if you still want it and it fits your plan, it may be a good buy.

exercises.prompt: 4 apples cost 2 gold. How much is one apple, in gold?
exercises.hint: Share the price equally between the apples.

exercises.prompt: A kite costs 6.50 gold at Tilly's stall and 5.75 gold at Bram's. How much cheaper is Bram's, in gold?
Sort these: a cost or a benefit of buying a bike?
items: that gold can't buy other things
exercises.hint: Costs are what you give up; benefits are what you get.
exercises.explain: Costs: the price, what else the gold could buy, and time fixing it. Benefits: speed, fun and fitness.

exercises.prompt: A rope costs 3 gold and lasts a day. Another costs 8 gold and lasts all year. You need a rope all year. Which is better value?
exercises.hint: How many 3-gold ropes would you need in a whole year?
exercises.explain: The 3-gold rope would need buying again and again; the 8-gold rope lasts all year, so it is better value.

exercises.prompt: Every gold coin can only be spent once.
exercises.hint: Can you spend the same coin on two things?
exercises.explain: True: once spent, the coin is gone, so every choice gives something up.

exercises.prompt: 6 apples cost 2.40 gold and 4 apples cost 2 gold. Which is better value?
exercises.hint: Work out the price for one in each pack.
exercises.explain: 2.40 ÷ 6 = 0.40 gold each, and 2 ÷ 4 = 0.50 gold each. The pack of 6 is better value, if you will eat them all.

exercises.prompt: The big pack is better value, but you need only 2 apples and the rest would go bad. What should you do?
exercises.hint: Is it good value if you throw half away?
exercises.explain: Better value only counts if you use it all. Buy what you need, and nothing is wasted.

exercises.prompt: Mimi has 10 gold and wants a hat (10 gold) and a book (10 gold). She buys the hat. What is her opportunity cost?
exercises.explain: The book: she chose the hat, so she gave up the book.

exercises.prompt: Bram has 10 gold. He buys a lantern for 4.25 gold. How much gold is left?
Zara wants a glider now, but she is saving for a saddle. What would a smart spender do?
exercises.hint: Remember costs, benefits and opportunity cost.
choices: think what she gives up, then choose
exercises.explain: If she buys the glider, the saddle is her opportunity cost. Thinking first helps her choose what matters more.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: a smart spending habit, or not?
items: working out the price for one
a big pack you will waste
spending all your gold at once
exercises.hint: Smart spenders compare, think and wait.
exercises.explain: Smart: comparing stalls, finding the price for one and waiting a day. Not smart: buying on a whim, wasting a big pack and spending everything at once.

play.hook: Two market stalls sell the same kite for different prices. Spend your gold wisely!
coach: Find the price for one to compare packs.
Cheapest is not always the best value.
Every gold coin can only be spent once.
Wait a day before buying something shiny.
play.world_task: At the shop, compare two stalls before you buy, and work out the price for one in any pack.
